title: Λύκοι καὶ κύνες ⟨πρὸς αὐτοὺς καταλλαγέντες⟩
titleEn: The Wolves and the Dogs Who Made Peace with Them
part: The Wolves and the Dogs Who Made Peace with Them (Chambry 216 · Perry 342)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 216 (= Perry 342). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Οἱ λύκοι τοῖς κυσὶν εἶπον· « Διὰ τί ὅμοιοι ὄντες ἡμῖν ἐν πᾶσιν, οὐχ ὁμοφρονεῖτε ἡμῖν ὡς ἀδελφοί ; οὐδὲν γὰρ ὑμῶν διαλλάττομεν, πλὴν τῇ γνώμῃ.
sentences.tr: Hoi lykoi tois kysin eipon· « Dia ti homoioi ontes hēmin en pasin, ouch homophroneite hēmin hōs adelphoi ; ouden gar hymōn diallattomen, plēn tēi gnōmēi.
sentences.l: The wolves said to the dogs: « Why, being like us in all things, are you not of-one-mind with us as brothers? For we differ in nothing from you, except in the way of thinking.
sentences.i: The wolves said to the dogs: « Why, when you are like us in every way, are you not of one mind with us as brothers? We differ from you in nothing but our thinking.
sentences.n: διαλλάττω with the genitive is "differ from", with οὐδέν as an accusative of respect, "in nothing". The wolves' whole argument turns on a likeness of body against a difference of γνώμη, and they treat the second as the trivial one — which the ending will not bear out. The speech opened here runs to the end of the third sentence.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν ἐλευθερίᾳ συζῶμεν· ὑμεῖς δὲ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ὑποκύπτοντες καὶ δουλεύοντες πληγὰς παρ’ αὐτῶν ὑπομένετε, καὶ κλοιὰ περιτίθεσθε, καὶ φυλάττετε τὰ πρόβατα· ὅτε δὲ ἐσθίουσιν, μόνα τὰ ὀστᾶ ὑμῖν ἐπιρρίπτουσιν.
sentences.tr: Kai hēmeis men eleutheriāi syzōmen· hymeis de tois anthrōpois hypokyptontes kai douleuontes plēgas par’ autōn hypomenete, kai kloia peritithesthe, kai phylattete ta probata· hote de esthiousin, mona ta osta hymin epirriptousin.
sentences.l: And we for our part live-with freedom; but you, stooping-under to men and slaving for them, endure blows from them, and put collars round yourselves, and guard the sheep; and when they eat, they throw on you the bones alone.
sentences.i: We live our lives in freedom, while you cringe before men and serve them, put up with beatings at their hands, take collars round your necks, and keep watch on their sheep — and when they eat, they throw you nothing but the bones.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς μέν … ὑμεῖς δέ sets the two lives side by side, the standard Greek way of drawing a contrast. συζάω is to share a life with something, and it takes the dative — freedom is the wolves' companion. ὑποκύπτω is to stoop down under something, the posture of the beaten and of the servant at once. περιτίθεσθε is middle — you put the collar round yourselves — so the wolves make even the collar the dogs' own doing. κλοιός is the dog-collar proper.

sentences.t: Ἀλλ’ ἐὰν πείθησθε, πάντα τὰ ποίμνια ἔκδοτε ἡμῖν καὶ ἕξομεν πάντα κοινὰ εἰς κόρον ἐσθίοντες. »
sentences.tr: All’ ean peithēsthe, panta ta poimnia ekdote hēmin kai hexomen panta koina eis koron esthiontes. »
sentences.l: But if you are-persuaded, hand over all the flocks to us, and we shall have all things in common, eating to satiety. »
sentences.i: But if you will listen to us, hand over all the flocks and we shall hold everything in common and eat our fill. »
sentences.n: ἐάν with the subjunctive is the vivid future condition, the offer put as a real prospect. πείθησθε is middle as much as passive: to be won over is to obey. εἰς κόρον is "to the point of surfeit". πάντα κοινά, "all things in common", is the language of friendship and of the ideal city — which makes it the exact language a swindle would borrow.

sentences.t: Ὑπήκουσαν οὖν πρὸς ταῦτα οἱ κύνες· οἱ δὲ ἔνδον τοῦ σπηλαίου εἰσελθόντες πρότερον τοὺς κύνας διέφθειραν.
sentences.tr: Hypēkousan oun pros tauta hoi kynes· hoi de endon tou spēlaiou eiselthontes proteron tous kynas diephtheiran.
sentences.l: So the dogs listened to these things; and the others, having-gone inside the cave, first destroyed the dogs.
sentences.i: So the dogs agreed to it; and the wolves, once they had got inside the cave, destroyed the dogs before anything else.
sentences.n: ὑπακούω is to listen from below and so to obey — the same stooping posture the wolves had just mocked. οἱ δέ shifts the subject back to the wolves without naming them, as Greek regularly does when the two parties alternate. πρότερον is the sting: before touching a single sheep.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ τὰς ἑαυτῶν πατρίδας προδιδόντες τοιούτους μισθοὺς λαμβάνουσι.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi tas heautōn patridas prodidontes toioutous misthous lambanousi.
sentences.l: That those betraying their own fatherlands receive such wages as these.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who betray their own countries receive wages such as these.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. τοιούτους points back at the massacre just told. μισθός is the wage of hired work, and calling the slaughter a wage is the whole of the irony.
